name: Elliptic de Sitter Space
description: De Sitter space with every event identified with the event opposite it on the hyperboloid, $X \sim -X$. One observer's horizon then bounds the whole world and future and past infinity are a single sphere. The spacetime has no closed timelike curves and no global direction of time.
convention: The de Sitter radius $\ell$ is a length, with $\Lambda = 3/\ell^2$, and we keep factors of $c$ explicit. An event is a pair of antipodal points $X$ and $-X$ of the hyperboloid $-X_0^2 + X_1^2 + X_2^2 + X_3^2 + X_4^2 = \ell^2$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Take a globe and call each point the same place as the point on the far side of it. Geometers know the result as elliptic space, and in 1917 Willem de Sitter listed it beside the sphere as one of the "two possible forms of space with constant positive curvature" [desitter1917]. On a sphere the straight lines that leave a point all meet again at its antipode, and in elliptic space two lines never share more than one point [desitter1917]. De Sitter judged it "really the simpler case" and wrote that "it is preferable to adopt this for the physical world" [desitter1917]. Einstein, he reported, had written to him with the same opinion [desitter1917].¶Does the trick work on a whole spacetime? De Sitter's own universe is the place to try it: drawn as a hyperboloid in flat space, a waist that narrows and widens again, it has for every event an opposite one on the far side of the waist [schrodinger1956]. Erwin Schrödinger took up "the so-called elliptic interpretation" in his book Expanding Universes of 1956, out of a worry about horizons: an observer in de Sitter space can explore only half of the hyperboloid, and which half depends on the path taken [schrodinger1956]. It struck him as "rather odd that two or more observers, even such as 'sat on the same school bench' in the remote past, should in future, when they have 'followed different paths in life', experience different worlds" [schrodinger1956]. His remedy was "declaring antipodes to represent the same event", after which any half of the hyperboloid that holds no antipodal pair "amounts to the whole world" [schrodinger1956].¶"But what price have we to pay for it?" he asked [schrodinger1956]. Draw an arrow of time on the world line of a particle, and the same particle at its antipodes carries the arrow reversed, one pointing up the hyperboloid and one down [schrodinger1956]. No way of cutting the hyperboloid in half settles which arrow is right, and "So the distinction between past and future is lost" [schrodinger1956]. Schrödinger found this "bewildering, but perhaps not absolutely fatal to the elliptic model" [schrodinger1956]. Particles and light obey reversible laws and need no arrow [schrodinger1956]. The trouble is with anything thermodynamic, an observer included, "carrying an innate arrow of time" [schrodinger1956].¶For the lost arrow the space hands something back: any two of its events can be joined by a geodesic, which fails in de Sitter space [hawking1973]. The two go together, by a theorem of 1962 due to Eugenio Calabi and Lawrence Markus: a space made by identifying points of de Sitter space joins every pair of events exactly when it has no direction of time [calabi1962, hawking1973]. To Stephen Hawking and George Ellis the antipodal map was "the simplest such identification" of de Sitter space, with a result that is "not time orientable" [hawking1973]. Gary Gibbons argued in 1986, for the same identification made on a black hole, that adopting it "would require giving up the complex structure of quantum mechanics and working with real Hilbert spaces" [gibbons1986elliptic]. On elliptic de Sitter space itself a quantum field is even or odd under the antipodal map, and Norma Sánchez found in 1987 that during inflation the fluctuation $\langle\phi^2\rangle$ of a scalar field then differs by a factor of 2 from the Bunch-Davies value [sanchez1987].¶In September 2002 Maulik Parikh, Ivo Savonije, and Erik Verlinde proposed that "for every event in de Sitter space, there is a CPT-conjugate event at its antipode", and called the result elliptic de Sitter space [parikh2003]. They read Schrödinger's remedy as observer complementarity, the principle taken over from black holes that each observer can describe everything inside the horizon with no loss of information: with antipodes identified, "every observer has complete information" [parikh2003]. An event and its antipode are spacelike separated, and their light cones never meet inside de Sitter space, so the identification makes no closed timelike curve [parikh2003]. Of each antipodal pair an observer sees exactly one, and at no finite time can any observer detect that events come doubled [parikh2003]. Future and past infinity, two spheres in de Sitter space, are a single sphere here, one boundary on which the three looked for a holographic description [parikh2003].¶The charts are de Sitter's own, the global, conformal, planar, static, and Kruskal coordinates that Marcus Spradlin, Andrew Strominger, and Anastasia Volovich set out in their Les Houches lectures of 2001 [spradlin2003]. In the global chart, where space is a sphere that shrinks and grows again, the identification sends each point of the sphere to the opposite point at the opposite time: $t \to -t$, $\chi \to \pi - \chi$ [parikh2003]. Half of space is then enough, $\chi \le \pi/2$, with the equator at the time $t$ glued to the equator at $-t$ [parikh2003]. For inflation with no beginning, Anthony Aguirre and Steven Gratton set the boundary conditions on a null surface of de Sitter space in January 2003, and wrote that their model "suggests, but does not require, the identification of antipodal points" [aguirre2003]. In that model the arrow of time is "well-defined and consistent for all physical observers that can communicate" [aguirre2003].

related.text: The hyperboloid before any points are identified, the double cover of this space. Every local measurement agrees with de Sitter's, and the two differ in topology alone [parikh2003].

Einstein's closed universe of 1917. Willem de Sitter proposed that year to take its space elliptic as well, opposite points of the sphere being one place, and reported that Einstein agreed [desitter1917].

Flat space with events identified under a boost, as de Sitter space is here under the antipodal map. Misner's identification makes closed timelike curves, and the antipodal one makes none [misner1967, parikh2003].

coordinates.name: Global

parameters.description: De Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = 3/\ell^2$; the sphere of space has its least radius, $\ell$, at $t = 0$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\chi$ the polar angle on the sphere of space, measured from the observer at $\chi = 0$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Conformal

parameters.description: De Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = 3/\ell^2$; the future and past infinities lie at $\eta = \pm\pi/2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\eta, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, all angles, with the conformal time $\eta$ related to the global chart by $\tan\eta = \sinh(ct/\ell)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Kruskal

parameters.description: De Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = 3/\ell^2$; the observer's horizons are $U = 0$ and $V = 0$, and a sphere of constant $U$ and $V$ has the areal radius $r = \ell(1 + UV)/(1 - UV)$

coordinates.convention: We use the null coordinates $U$ and $V$, both dimensionless and both increasing to the future in the static patch $U < 0 < V$ of the observer at $UV = -1$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Static

parameters.description: De Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = 3/\ell^2$; the cosmological horizon of the observer at $r = 0$ sits at $r = \ell$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} - \dfrac{r\left(\ell + r\right)\left(\ell - r\right)}{\ell^4}\dot{t}^2 + \dfrac{r}{\left(\ell + r\right)\left(\ell - r\right)}\dot{r}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(\ell + r\right)\left(\ell - r\right)}{\ell^2}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(\ell + r\right)\left(\ell - r\right)\sin^2\theta}{\ell^2}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Planar

parameters.description: De Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = 3/\ell^2$; the expansion rate of the flat slices is $H = c/\ell$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ comoving lengths. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
